Content:
To solve an equation with a decimal coefficient, such as
[MATH: 0.2x = -1,]

Content:
we start by getting rid of the decimal. To do this, we multiply both sides of the equation by [MATH: {\color{blue}10}.] Multiplying a decimal by [MATH: 10] shifts the decimal place one spot over to the right.

Content:
[MATH: 0.2x|= − 1; 10 ⋅ (0.2x)|= 10 ⋅ (− 1); 2x|= − 10]

Content:
Then, we solve the equation using the multiplication principle, as usual:

Content:
[MATH: 2x|= − 10; (2x)/(2)|= (− 10)/(2); (2x)/(2)|= − (10)/(2); x|= − 5]

items.readable_text:
Content:
How do we get rid of the decimal in an equation like

Content:
[MATH: 0.25x = 2,]

Content:
when there is more than one number behind the decimal place? If we multiply by [MATH: 10] as usual, we shift the decimal place over one spot to the right:

Content:
[MATH: 0.25x|= 2; 10 ⋅ (0.25x)|= 10 ⋅ (2); 2.5x|= 20]

Content:
However, there is still one number behind the decimal place. So, we can multiply by [MATH: 10] again:

Content:
[MATH: 2.5x|= 20; 10 ⋅ (2.5x)|= 10 ⋅ (20); 25x|= 200]

Content:
Now that our equation contains only whole numbers, we can continue with the usual method of applying the multiplication principle:

Content:
[MATH: 25x|= 200; (25x)/(25)|= (200)/(25); (25x)/(25)|= (200)/(25); x|= 8]

Content:
Looking back, we can see a faster way to apply the same method. We multiplied by [MATH: 10] twice, which means that overall, we multiplied by [MATH: 100.] In general, multiplying a decimal by [MATH: 100] shifts the decimal place over two spots to the right. So, we could have solved the equation faster by multiplying by [MATH: 100.]

Content:
[MATH: 0.25x|= 2; 100 ⋅ (0.25x)|= 100 ⋅ (2); 25x|= 200; (25x)/(25)|= (200)/(25); (25x)/(25)|= (200)/(25); x|= 8]

Content:

[MATH: 0.2x = -1,]

we start by getting rid of the decimal. To do this, we multiply both sides of the equation by [MATH: {\color{blue}10}.] Multiplying a decimal by [MATH: 10] shifts the decimal place one spot over to the right.

Content:

Content:
Then, we solve the equation using the multiplication principle, as usual:

Content:
[MATH: 2x|= − 10; (2x)/(2)|= (− 10)/(2); (2x)/(2)|= − (10)/(2); x|= − 5]
